explanations.explanation: Titus it is, friend. Paul says, "I had no peace in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus there." Open door, and his mind is on the one friend who isn't in the room. I think that tells you how much Titus mattered to him.

Timothy is named right alongside Paul at the start of this letter (2 Corinthians 1:1), so I see why he came to mind. But in Troas, the one Paul says he didn't find was "my brother Titus." Two T names, one missing friend. I mix up names in my own bakery, so no shame here.

Silas was a coworker Paul chose to travel with (Acts 15:40), so it's a real name from his journeys. He just isn't the name in this verse. Paul says he had no peace "because I did not find my brother Titus there." Titus is the one who was missing in Troas.

explanations.answer: Says goodbye and goes on to Macedonia
explanations.explanation: That's what Paul says. He told the people in Troas goodbye and went on to Macedonia. A door was standing open, and he still left without peace in his spirit. I think that's a man who couldn't settle with his friend missing.

explanations.answer: Stays in Troas and keeps on preaching
explanations.explanation: I get the pull. An open door sounds like a reason to stay put. But Paul says he said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia. The text doesn't tell us he kept preaching in Troas after that.

explanations.answer: Sails straight back across to Corinth
explanations.explanation: Paul is writing to the Corinthians, so Corinth makes sense as a guess. But he says he said goodbye and "went on to Macedonia." That's the next stop in this verse, and Corinth isn't mentioned as one.

Yes, friend. God "through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of the knowledge of Him." Think about walking past a bakery. You don't need a sign, your nose already knows something good is going on in there.

explanations.answer: The sound of His great name
explanations.explanation: A great name does deserve a great sound, I'll give you that. But Paul isn't talking about sound here. He says God spreads "the fragrance of the knowledge of Him." This verse is all about what you can smell.

explanations.answer: The light of His holy law
explanations.explanation: Light and law are both big Bible words, so I see the pick. But in this verse Paul says God spreads "the fragrance of the knowledge of Him." It's something you smell, not something you see. Paul doesn't mention the law here at all.

Close, but Paul says more than that. He says, "we are to God the sweet aroma of Christ among those who are being saved and those who are perishing." That's both groups, not just one. The aroma goes out to everybody in range.

Right, because Paul says it covers two groups. He says they are "the sweet aroma of Christ among those who are being saved and those who are perishing." That aroma isn't locked in one room. It goes out to both.

Life is the word. Paul says, "To the one we are an odor that brings death, to the other a fragrance that brings life." Same aroma going out, two different results. Paul is the one saying it, so I just read it out loud.
Rest sounds lovely, friend. I could use some myself after a long batch. But Paul sets death next to something else: "a fragrance that brings life." Death on one side, life on the other.

Honor is a nice word, but it isn't the one Paul uses. He says to the one group they're "an odor that brings death," and to the other "a fragrance that brings life." Death and life sit side by side in that verse.

It's actually the opposite. Paul says, "we are not like so many others, who peddle the word of God for profit." Picture someone selling dough out of a trunk in a parking lot. Paul says that's not him and his team.

That's it. Paul says, "we are not like so many others, who peddle the word of God for profit." Instead he says, "in Christ we speak before God with sincerity, as men sent from God." Not a salesman's pitch, just sincere speaking.
Yep. Paul says, "You yourselves are our letter, inscribed on our hearts, known and read by everyone." The people he was writing to are the letter. That's some real mail, friend.

Titus, the brother Paul missed in Troas (2 Corinthians 2:13), is a fair name to remember here. But when Paul talks about his letter, he says to the Corinthians, "You yourselves are our letter." He's pointing right at the people reading his words.
Jerusalem is a big name, so I see why it came up. But Paul doesn't mention it in this passage. He says to the Corinthians, "You yourselves are our letter, inscribed on our hearts."

explanations.answer: The Spirit of the living God
explanations.explanation: That's what Paul says. The letter is "written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God." You can't buy that at an office supply store, friend.

explanations.answer: The blood of the faithful prophets
explanations.explanation: That one sounds serious, I know. But Paul never mentions blood or prophets in this passage. He says the letter is "written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God."

explanations.answer: The oil used to anoint kings
explanations.explanation: Oil is a good guess, since it's a real Bible thing for anointing kings (1 Samuel 16:13). But Paul isn't using it here. He says the letter is "written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God."
Hearts, friend. Paul says the letter is written "not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts." Stone is hard and stays in one place. A heart goes with you everywhere.
Clay is a real writing surface, so it's a fair guess. But Paul says the letter is written "not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts." The writing is on people, not on pottery.
Gold would make one shiny letter. I like the thinking. But Paul says it's written "not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts." Hearts are worth more than gold anyway, if you ask me.

That's what Paul says. He writes, "Not that we are competent in ourselves to claim that anything comes from us, but our competence comes from God." It's honest, and it takes the pressure off. Nobody has to bake the whole batch on their own strength.

It's the other way around. Paul says, "Not that we are competent in ourselves to claim that anything comes from us, but our competence comes from God." He isn't taking the credit. He points it straight at God.
New is the word. Paul says God "has qualified us as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit." Notice who does the qualifying. It's God, not Paul.

Old is a sensible guess, since Paul does bring up tablets of stone in the verses just before. But he says God has qualified them as ministers of a "new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit." New is the word he picks.
Royal sounds fancy, like it needs a good apron. But Paul says God has qualified them "as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit." He never calls it royal.
